title: Real-time decoding of quantum error correction codes using high-performance computing
authors: Lingling Lao, Qiang Wang, Yuanqi Liu, Yantong Liu, Haowen Wang, Yitao Chen, Yankang Zhao, Zhenwei Wu, Wei Zhang, Yong Dong, Yingwen Liu, Mingche Lai, Junjie Wu
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is indispensable for building scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers. Effective QEC demands stringent real-time decoding: the decoder must process syndrome measurements and determine corrections within a time scale--typically on the order of microseconds, to avoid data backlog. Scaling to large number of logical qubits further necessitates significant computational resources. In this work, we propose an architecture, called \emph{THQLink}, for real-time decoding of quantum error correction codes using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The network connecting the HPC and the control system of quantum processing unit (QPU) is built on TH-Express and can be adapted to different quantum technologies and their associated control stacks. We report a round-trip latency of 2.944 $μ$s on average, with an incremental overhead of 130 ns per additional hop. Using a parallel window strategy, we demonstrate real-time decoding (1 $μ$s per QEC round) of the surface code up to distance 19 using a matching-based decoder on CPUs. Our work presents a scalable framework for real-time decoding in fault-tolerant quantum computing. It can be readily applied to quantum-centric supercomputers that feature tight integration between QPU and HPC resources, thereby enabling efficient support for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms and computation-intensive workloads offloaded from the QPU.
summary: This paper introduces THQLink, an architecture designed to enable real-time Quantum Error Correction (QEC) decoding using coupled High-Performance Computing and QPU resources. By implementing a parallel window decoding strategy, the authors overcome the latency limitations of traditional decoders, enabling scalable fault tolerance for large quantum codes.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving real-time decoding of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes, which requires processing syndrome measurements within microsecond timescales to prevent computational backlogs.
main_result: The proposed THQLink architecture successfully demonstrates real-time decoding for the surface code up to distance 19 by integrating HPC resources with the QPU via a low-latency interconnect.
method: The authors propose an architectural framework (THQLink) and compare different decoding strategies, notably developing a parallel-window decoder that scales better than global batch decoders in terms of latency vs. code distance.
model_or_system: The work focuses on the surface code model for QEC, which protects logical qubits using physical qubits arranged on a 2D lattice. The implementation relies on coupling quantum processors (QPU) with general-purpose High-Performance Computing (HPC) resources.
key_observables: Round-trip latency ($\mu$s), decoding time per round ($1 \mu s$), logical error rate ($	ext{P}_{	ext{fail}}$), and code distance ($d$).
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($p$) (e.g., 0.1%, 0.3%), Code Distance ($d$), and the required real-time constraint ($\sim 1 \mu s$).
main_assumptions: The parallel window decoding strategy trades a slight increase in logical error rate for a substantial reduction in latency, which is necessary for large code distances.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the THQLink architecture and closed-loop data flow. Comparisons show that while global decoders fail to meet real-time constraints beyond moderate distances, the parallel window decoder maintains throughput by overlapping syndrome rounds.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of low-latency QEC decoding. It then details the THQLink architecture and its performance metrics. Finally, it compares advanced decoding algorithms (Global vs. Parallel Window) to demonstrate scalable real-time operation for large surface codes.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing by providing a concrete, high-throughput hardware/software framework for error correction decoding.
